title: FRM Operational, Lesson 3: Model risk and third-party risk
subtitle: When the instrument that measures risk becomes a source of it - and why internal control does not stop at the edge of the organisation
whyItMatters: Every VaR number, every credit rating, every pricing model rests on assumptions - and assumptions can be wrong. Model risk is the risk that the very tool used to measure and manage other risks turns into the origin of the loss. It became a central topic after 2008, when a whole generation of CDO pricing models was shown to be wrong in the same systematic way.
openingQuestion: Where does model risk come from?
openingOptions: Only from coding errors inside the model's implementation
From wrong assumptions and input data that does not represent the future
Only from machine learning models, never from traditional statistical models
Model risk is a theoretical concern that has never caused a material loss in practice
explanation: Model risk has three main sources: (1) a wrong foundational assumption - the low-correlation assumption baked into pre-2008 CDO models, for instance; (2) input data that does not represent the future - calibrating on a calm period and then forecasting a crisis; (3) a model used outside the scope it was designed for - applying a European option pricing model to an American-style option without adjusting for early exercise.

diagram.label: A model is built on assumptions plus historical data
The assumption is wrong, or the data does not represent what comes next
The model returns a wrong answer that still looks rigorous and scientific
Decisions taken on that wrong answer produce a real loss

realWorldExample.description: JPMorgan's Chief Investment Office switched to a new VaR model for a complex credit derivatives book. Because of implementation errors - including a spreadsheet formula that divided by the wrong figure - the new model reported materially less risk than the position actually carried. The position was allowed to grow on the strength of that understated VaR, and when the market moved against it the bank lost more than 6bn USD. It is one of the cleanest illustrations of model risk there is: the market did not do anything unimaginable, the instrument measuring the risk was simply wrong.

quiz.question: In JPMorgan's "London Whale" episode, what was the direct source of the loss?
options: A market event so unexpected that no risk model anywhere in the world, however sophisticated, could have anticipated or priced it in advance
Deliberate accounting fraud committed by senior management to conceal the true size of the credit derivatives book
A new VaR model with implementation errors that understated risk, letting the position grow far too large before anyone noticed
A cyber attack that corrupted the trade data feeding the desk's risk reporting and position keeping systems
quiz.explanation: This is model risk in its purest form: the tool used to control risk (VaR) is itself the origin of the problem, because it misstated how much risk was actually being carried, and every decision taken on that number - above all the decision to allow a larger position - was therefore wrong. Nothing here required an unimaginable market move, deliberate concealment or an outside attacker; the market moved within a normal range and the arithmetic inside the model was simply wrong, which is precisely why independent validation exists.

quiz.question: Why is "a model applied outside its design scope" an important source of model risk?
options: Because any model at all can be applied to any asset class you like without adjustment of any kind, as the underlying mathematics is identical
Because regulators forbid outright the reuse of any existing model for any product it was not originally built, tested and approved for
Because it is a purely theoretical concern that never arises in live operation on a real trading desk carrying real open positions
Because a model calibrated and validated for one asset class and one set of market conditions can return badly wrong answers in a different context if nobody revalidates it
quiz.explanation: Take Black-Scholes: it assumes constant volatility and no unusual dividends. Apply it to an option whose behaviour departs sharply from those assumptions, without adjusting anything, and the price it returns is wrong even though the mathematics of the formula contains no error at all. That is what makes this source so hard to catch. Nobody forbids reuse and no model refuses to run; the failure is silent, and it happens in live books, not in textbooks.

quiz.question: What is the key ingredient of effective model risk management?
options: An independent validation team, separate from the builders, that reviews assumptions, data and scope before the model is used for decisions
The team that built the model reviewing its own code and documentation carefully before go-live, since nobody else understands the mathematics as well
Writing the model in the most modern programming language available, so that the code runs fast and stays easy to read
No further validation once a model has been in service for several years without ever producing an obviously bad number
quiz.explanation: The principle mirrors the three lines of defence: the team that builds a model (line one) should not be the only team that judges it. An independent validation function (line two) checks the assumptions, the quality of the data, and whether the model is being used inside the scope it was designed for - including for models that have been running for years, because market conditions move underneath them. Choice of programming language is irrelevant to whether the assumptions hold, and long service is a reason to revalidate rather than an exemption from it.

quiz.question: In a modern operating environment, third-party risk is mainly about what?
options: Only the legal risk that arises when drafting and then signing the commercial contracts with the external service providers based outside the organisation
The risk that an outside supplier the organisation depends on fails, causing disruption or loss to the organisation even though the fault lies elsewhere
A category that applies to technology companies but has no real bearing on how a regulated bank runs its operations
A risk that only exists where the counterparty to the outsourcing contract is foreign rather than a domestic firm
quiz.explanation: The CrowdStrike outage in the previous lesson illustrated this exactly: the defect sat with the supplier, but the operational and reputational consequences belonged to every organisation that used the service. Managing third-party risk therefore means assessing the resilience of critical suppliers, not just signing a contract and filing it. Contract law is one control among several rather than the whole discipline, banks are among the most dependent users of outsourced infrastructure, and a domestic supplier can fail exactly as a foreign one can.

quiz.question: Why is using a model outside the scope it was designed for such a large source of risk?
options: Because the new users are usually never trained on how the model works at all
Because the model runs a great deal more slowly on any out-of-scope data
Because it still returns a plausible-looking number and warns nobody
Because a regulator must re-approve the model for every single new scope of use
quiz.explanation: A corporate bond pricing model will happily return a number when you feed it a structured product - it has no way of knowing that its underlying assumptions have stopped holding. There is no error message, no failed run, nothing that looks different from a normal day. That silence is exactly why model risk management insists that the permitted scope of use is written into the model's own documentation, and why a control fires when somebody takes the model outside it.

practicePrompt.question: A pricing model was built and validated for liquid corporate bonds. Another desk starts using it for small, thinly traded corporate issues. Which source of model risk is this?
options: The right model used in the wrong place - outside its design scope
A wrong foundational assumption, since the pricing formula is unsound
Unrepresentative data, because the training sample is far too old now
Not model risk at all, since the model was fully validated beforehand
practicePrompt.explanation: The three sources of model risk need three different remedies, so naming the source correctly is the first step. Here the model is not wrong and the data is not wrong - it was built properly for one asset class and is being used on another, where the assumptions about liquidity and about the reliability of reference prices no longer hold. No amount of revalidation would catch this, because validation only asks whether the model does well the job it was designed to do. The remedy is a model inventory that records permitted scope, and a control that fires when somebody steps outside it.

keyTakeaways: Model risk has three sources: a wrong foundational assumption, data that does not represent the future, and a model used outside its design scope
London Whale (JPMorgan, 2012): implementation errors in a new VaR model understated risk, letting the position grow before it lost more than 6bn USD
Model risk management needs an independent validation team, separate from the builders - including for models that have been in service for years
Third-party risk extends the perimeter of internal control past the edge of the organisation, out to critical suppliers the firm does not directly control

summary.keyIdea: Model risk has three distinct sources - a wrong assumption, unrepresentative data, and the right model used in the wrong place - so it needs three different remedies rather than one generic process.
summary.commonMistake: Letting the team that built a model validate its own work. London Whale was an implementation error, and it survived because nobody independent ever looked.

application.title: Past the edge of the organisation
application.message: List the suppliers whose failure would stop your service. The list is usually shorter than expected, and far more concentrated.

sections.text: There is a paradox at the centre of modern risk management: the instruments built to measure and control risk - the VaR model, the credit rating model, the pricing model - can themselves be the origin of the loss, if nobody checks the assumptions inside them independently.

items: A wrong foundational assumption - the model is mathematically correct but rests on a premise that no longer matches reality
Unrepresentative input data - calibrating the model on a calm period and then using it to forecast a crisis
Application outside the design scope - reusing a model for a different product or market condition than intended, without revalidating it

sections.label: What London Whale actually teaches
sections.text: The striking part of the JPMorgan episode is not the size of the loss but the fact that the model error - including a basic spreadsheet formula mistake - went undetected until the position had grown beyond control. That is why model risk management is now a distinct area within the Basel framework, with independent validation as a hard requirement.

lines: No model is perfect - the right question is not "is this model correct" but "who checks it independently, and how often."
Operational Resilience ends here; the next stage turns to a different kind of risk, one that was underestimated until it very nearly brought down the entire banking system in 2008 - liquidity risk.
